title: Theosis (CCC 460)
hook: the Son of God became man so that we might share his divinity

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Armenian Catholics, and Gregory brought up from the pit to pray over the king who put him there. Your line was the first nation. Whose story did you see differently? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-eight.

Ask a room of churchgoers why God became man, and the answers come quickly. To forgive our sins. To show us the way. To die for us. All of those are in the Catechism. But the Catechism doesn't stop there. In one short paragraph, number four hundred sixty, it gives a reason that is easy to read past: the Word became flesh to make us partakers of the divine nature. Not just forgiven. Not just shown the way. Brought into God's own life. The Eastern churches we've been visiting have a word for this, and they treasure it. Today, that word.
screen: `TO FORGIVE, TO SHOW THE WAY.` → `AND ONE MORE REASON.` → `PARTAKERS OF THE DIVINE NATURE.`

segments.voice: Underneath the paragraph is a line from scripture. The Second Letter of Peter says, in the Douay-Rheims, that God has given us most great and precious promises, "that by these you may be made partakers of the divine nature." A partaker is someone who has a share. Not an owner. A sharer. Next, the saints the Catechism calls as witnesses. It quotes Saint Irenaeus, Saint Athanasius and Saint Thomas Aquinas, West and East side by side, all saying the same startling thing. Athanasius's line, in an old English translation, is short enough to memorize: "For He was made man that we might be made God." Then the careful part, because that line can be heard wrong. It doesn't mean people become a second God, or stop being creatures, or dissolve into God like sugar in tea. Eastern writers explain it with a picture: iron left in a fire. It glows, it burns, it gives off heat and light, and it's still iron. The fire is the fire's own; the iron shares it. That's theosis: being drawn into God's life by grace, while remaining yourself, a creature, a person. Last, why the Eastern churches care so much about it. It sheds light on what we've seen these past days. The icons show saints already shining with that light. The liturgy is heaven touching earth. Babies receive communion, and God's life is offered from the start. Catholics in the West tend to say grace, sanctification, or sharing in the divine life. Catholics in the East say theosis. The Catechism puts both vocabularies on one page.
screen: `PARTAKERS OF THE DIVINE NATURE.` · `IRENAEUS, ATHANASIUS, AQUINAS.` · `IRON IN THE FIRE: GLOWING, STILL IRON.` · `ONE PAGE, TWO VOCABULARIES.` · then, large: `HE WAS MADE MAN THAT WE MIGHT BE MADE GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with that sentence. Settle, and breathe. Let the line come back slowly: he was made man that we might be made God. Don't analyze it. Notice which word catches. Man. Made. God. We. Stay with that one word for a few breaths. If the picture helps, think of the iron in the fire, still iron, glowing. If you pray, you can simply rest in the line, words the Church has kept. If you don't, let it be a sentence someone believed enough to stake a life on, and keep it company. The bell holds the time.
Theosis. The Eastern Christian word for being drawn into God's own life by grace, made partakers of the divine nature while remaining creatures. Today's word.

Your line: made sharers. Today, when you share something, a meal, a seat, a story, remember the word partaker, and how much the Catechism says has been shared. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Eastern Catholics, like the Orthodox, speak of theosis as the goal of the Christian life; Latin Catholics usually speak of grace and sharing in the divine life, and the Catechism (CCC 460) presents both together.

fork.setup: a friend hears "he was made man that we might be made God" and asks if Christians think they'll become gods. what does the tradition say?
options: yes, each person becomes a separate god.
no: by grace we share God's life and remain creatures.
it's only poetry and means nothing.
fork.reveal: Eastern and Western Christians alike read it as sharing in God's life by grace. the iron glows with the fire, and stays iron.

original.note: Greek: deification, being drawn into God's life; the Eastern Christian word for what CCC 460 describes.

trapdoor: what you thought: theosis sounds like people turning into God.
what it means: by grace, people become sharers in God's own life, while remaining creatures.

what a scholar hears: CCC 460 gathers 2 Peter 1:4, Irenaeus, Athanasius (On the Incarnation 54) and Aquinas; the distinction between God's essence and the grace shared is how theologians keep creature and Creator distinct.

notes: CCC 460 paraphrased (the Word became flesh to make us partakers of the divine nature; citations of 2 Peter 1:4, Irenaeus, Athanasius and Aquinas). The Catechism's wording is copyrighted, so nothing is quoted from it. The paragraph number is the cited text's own.
Athanasius quoted from the Schaff NPNF (Robertson) translation of De Incarnatione 54.3: confirm exact wording 'For He was made man that we might be made God.'
The iron-in-fire image is a traditional Eastern illustration (e.g. Maximus the Confessor, John of Damascus); not attributed to a single source. Confirm.
'Catholics in the West tend to say grace, sanctification' is a general description, not a ranking; confirm it is fair.

Editor: paraphrase of 2 Peter 1:4 aligned with the Douay-Rheims ('most great and precious promises'); cut the line telling the listener a careful reader will 'stop and read it twice'; 'Eastern Christians explain' narrowed to 'Eastern writers'; 'it shapes everything' and the causal claim about infant communion softened; teach opener varied.
